sources.label: Document A · Declaration of Independence
sources.title: Declaration of Independence
sources.creator: Second Continental Congress
sources.excerpt: The Declaration argues that governments derive just powers from consent; it announces political ideals and independence, not an enforceable federal constitution.
sources.limitation: This summary describes the linked source's scope; consult the document itself for exact language, date and purpose. Context readings are separate instructional interpretations.
sources.lessonContext: Locke's social-contract arguments challenged unlimited monarchy by asking why political authority is legitimate. Natural-rights reasoning holds that certain rights do not depend on a ruler's gift, while consent of the governed requires government to answer to the people. Enlightenment authors disagreed about representation, property, religion and who qualified as a political member. Their arguments should be studied in their historical context, including exclusions they did not remedy.

sources.label: Document B · Constitution
sources.title: Constitution
sources.creator: Constitutional Convention
sources.excerpt: The Preamble and articles establish a proposed structure of government. Compare the document's promises with rules about representation and ratification.
sources.limitation: This summary describes the linked source's scope; consult the document itself for exact language, date and purpose. Context readings are separate instructional interpretations.
sources.lessonContext: The Declaration of Independence was adopted by the Second Continental Congress in 1776. It states political principles concerning equality, rights, consent and the right to alter a destructive government. Its list of grievances makes an argument against British rule and addresses audiences at home and abroad. Unlike the Constitution, it did not create the operating branches of the later federal government.

sources.label: Document C · Maryland Government Framework
sources.title: Maryland Government Framework
sources.creator: Maryland State Department of Education
sources.excerpt: The state framework provides inquiry and assessment expectations, not an original founding-period document.
sources.limitation: This summary describes the linked source's scope; consult the document itself for exact language, date and purpose. Context readings are separate instructional interpretations.
sources.lessonContext: Popular sovereignty places ultimate political authority in the people. Republican government uses representatives selected through established political rules, while constitutionalism limits the powers of public officials. The rule of law requires government action to follow legal constraints; it does not mean every law or decision is automatically fair. These principles can reinforce one another or come into tension.

questions.prompt: Which evidence would best support an analysis of natural-rights ideas influencing later government?
choices: Assume every Enlightenment writer supported identical voting rights.
Use only a modern slogan without examining its historical meaning.
Compare a dated Enlightenment argument with passages of a later founding document and identify both agreement and limits.
questions.explain: The best response uses the appropriate source, legal authority, context and evidence, instead of treating a slogan or unsupported inference as proof.

questions.prompt: Which research method best evaluates a tension between the Declaration's ideals and society in 1776?
choices: Dismiss the political text as useless because its promises were not universally fulfilled.
Compare its stated principles with contemporary law and experiences of people excluded from political rights.
Infer that every adult could vote immediately after July 1776.
questions.explain: The best response uses the appropriate source, legal authority, context and evidence, instead of treating a slogan or unsupported inference as proof.

questions.prompt: A city council passes a popular ordinance that conflicts with constitutional protections. Which conclusion is strongest?
choices: Majority support matters but cannot alone authorize government to violate constitutional rights.
A popular ordinance cannot face court review.
Only judges determine every policy choice regardless of elections.
questions.explain: The best response uses the appropriate source, legal authority, context and evidence, instead of treating a slogan or unsupported inference as proof.

questions.prompt: A representative claims their authority comes only from birthright. Which founding principle challenges that claim?
choices: Hereditary power is a constitutional requirement for every office.
The rule of law permits officeholders to ignore ordinary legal limits.
Consent of the governed requires political power to be justified to the people.
questions.explain: Consent-based government does not treat heredity as sufficient political legitimacy.

questions.prompt: The Declaration argues for independence while the Constitution establishes federal institutions. Which comparison is defensible?
choices: The Constitution was adopted before the Declaration was written.
The Declaration creates the three modern federal branches.
They are different kinds of documents, one announcing reasons for separation and one structuring federal government.
questions.explain: Their purposes and legal roles differ.

questions.prompt: Why might a political principle receive broad public support but still require constitutional limits?
choices: Because popularity always creates legal authority.
Because the Constitution has no relationship to the public.
Because elected institutions must also respect individual rights and valid law.
questions.explain: Majorities and constitutional protections are both relevant.

matchingPrompts.prompt: Which founding document argues that political independence is justified by violations of rights and consent?
Which founding document establishes the later federal government's constitutional structure?
Which source describes the state's current inquiry and assessment expectations rather than eighteenth-century ideas?

10.1.inquiryPrompt: How should constitutional principles and credible evidence guide decisions about foundations of democracy?
inquirySteps: Compare the identified public institutions, original texts and their limitations.
Develop an inquiry question about a specific civic decision, right or policy.
Defend a qualified conclusion using evidence, limits and a possible counterargument.
conclusions: A credible civic argument should identify the governing rule, affected people and evidence that could test its impact.
Because a government source states a goal, the goal must already have been achieved equally in every community.
The foundations of democracy unit requires distinguishing source claims from evidence of real-world effects.
10.1.writing: Evaluate a civic dispute or constitutional question connected to Foundations of Democracy. Develop a qualified thesis using at least two relevant documents or authoritative references. Explain which level or branch of government has authority, which rights or public values are at issue, the evidence supporting your interpretation, a counterargument and one significant evidence limitation.
10.1.challenge: Civic Policy Lab: create a nonpartisan brief or mock hearing packet about Foundations of Democracy. Identify the decision-making body, make a sourced recommendation, compare at least two affected perspectives, and propose measurable outcomes.
10.1.standards: Maryland 2025 American Government Framework — civics inquiry, constitutional institutions, participation and applicable unit skills. Exact indicator mapping requires review.
10.1.sourceAudit: Three linked original constitutional/legal records or official interpretive resources. Source summaries are educational paraphrases and do not substitute for document excerpts.
10.1.sampleAnswer:
The civic question in Foundations of Democracy involves who has legitimate authority and what limits that authority. A strong answer identifies a specific governmental act, legal principle and affected community, rather than assuming a popular decision is automatically constitutional.

Source A, Declaration of Independence, provides the starting rule or historical context. Source B, Constitution, adds another institutional perspective. These records must be read with their creators and dates in mind; the fact that an institution announced a goal does not prove the goal was achieved.

A third source, Maryland Government Framework, can help clarify the competing obligations, evidence or limits of the case. An informed conclusion should test stated intentions against official records and relevant outcomes, while recognizing that some sources represent officials more directly than ordinary residents.

A reasonable counterargument may prioritize another constitutional value, public benefit or interpretation. The strongest recommendation considers that opposing claim, explains why some evidence is more persuasive and identifies what new information could change the decision.

sources.label: Document A · Constitution — Articles I–III
sources.title: Constitution — Articles I–III
sources.creator: Constitutional Convention
sources.excerpt: The articles distribute legislative, executive and judicial powers; constitutional powers and actual institutional influence should be examined separately.
sources.limitation: This summary describes the linked source's scope; consult the document itself for exact language, date and purpose. Context readings are separate instructional interpretations.
sources.lessonContext: Delegates met in Philadelphia in 1787 after difficulties under the Articles of Confederation. They debated representation, federal powers, slavery and the balance between national and state authority. The Connecticut Compromise helped create different representation rules for the House and Senate, while the Three-Fifths Clause strengthened slaveholding states' representation without granting enslaved people political rights.

sources.label: Document B · Federalist No. 51
sources.title: Federalist No. 51
sources.creator: James Madison (under the name Publius)
sources.excerpt: Madison defended checks among branches; this is an argument for ratification, not proof that checks always work as designed.
sources.limitation: This summary describes the linked source's scope; consult the document itself for exact language, date and purpose. Context readings are separate instructional interpretations.
sources.lessonContext: Federalism divides responsibilities between national and state governments, while separation of powers distributes federal authority among legislative, executive and judicial branches. These are different arrangements. Congress legislates within constitutional authority; the president executes federal law; federal courts resolve cases within their jurisdiction.

sources.label: Document C · Bill of Rights
sources.title: Bill of Rights
sources.creator: U.S. Congress / ratifying states
sources.excerpt: The first ten amendments set protections and constraints on federal power; later amendments and case law shaped their application.
sources.limitation: This summary describes the linked source's scope; consult the document itself for exact language, date and purpose. Context readings are separate instructional interpretations.
sources.lessonContext: Checks and balances give institutions ways to limit other institutions while performing their own assigned responsibilities. The president may veto legislation; Congress may override a veto by the required supermajority; the Senate exercises advice-and-consent powers for certain appointments and treaties. Courts may review governmental actions in cases properly before them.

questions.prompt: Which evidence best supports a nuanced evaluation of the Constitutional Convention?
choices: Read only a modern summary of the word compromise.
Compare proposed plans, convention debates and the final compromises, noting who had no seat in the debates.
Treat the finished Constitution as proof that delegates never disagreed.
questions.explain: The best response uses the appropriate source, legal authority, context and evidence, instead of treating a slogan or unsupported inference as proof.

questions.prompt: A state and federal rule conflict over a regulated issue. What must a student establish first?
choices: Identify the constitutional authority for each rule and whether the federal rule is valid in the relevant field.
Assume state policy automatically wins because schools are local.
Assume every federal announcement overrides the Constitution.
questions.explain: The best response uses the appropriate source, legal authority, context and evidence, instead of treating a slogan or unsupported inference as proof.

questions.prompt: Congress wants to enact a bill despite a presidential veto. What demonstrates the constitutional check?
choices: The Supreme Court must rewrite the bill before a vote.
The vice president alone can sign the vetoed bill into law.
Both houses can attempt a two-thirds override under Article I.
questions.explain: The best response uses the appropriate source, legal authority, context and evidence, instead of treating a slogan or unsupported inference as proof.

questions.prompt: A proposal would directly change the constitutional text. Which path is appropriate?
choices: Require only a presidential press release and no ratification.
Follow the amendment procedures in Article V rather than treating an ordinary statute as a textual amendment.
Have one federal judge rewrite the Constitution without a case.
questions.explain: The best response uses the appropriate source, legal authority, context and evidence, instead of treating a slogan or unsupported inference as proof.

questions.prompt: A proposed reform changes the actual words of the federal Constitution. Which action is required?
choices: A presidential order that is published once.
Article V proposal and ratification procedures.
A simple committee vote in the House.
questions.explain: Formal amendment is distinct from legislation or interpretation.

questions.prompt: Which fact best distinguishes federalism from separation of powers?
choices: They are names for the same power held by judges alone.
Federalism means the president controls all state legislatures.
Federalism divides authority between national and state levels; separation allocates roles among branches.
questions.explain: The arrangements distribute power in different directions.

matchingPrompts.prompt: Which original text assigns legislative, executive and judicial authority?
Which essay defends institutional checks against concentrations of power during the ratification debate?
Which adopted amendments provide early explicit protections against federal governmental action?

lessons.essential: How can we use credible sources and constitutional reasoning to investigate how congress is organized?

lessons.essential: How can we use credible sources and constitutional reasoning to investigate how a bill becomes law?

lessons.essential: How can we use credible sources and constitutional reasoning to investigate congressional representation and oversight?

sources.label: Document A · Constitution Article I
sources.title: Constitution Article I
sources.creator: Constitutional Convention
sources.excerpt: Article I gives legislative power to a bicameral Congress; a law's passage requires multiple institutional stages.
sources.limitation: This summary describes the linked source's scope; consult the document itself for exact language, date and purpose. Context readings are separate instructional interpretations.
sources.lessonContext: Congress has two chambers: the House of Representatives, apportioned among states by population, and the Senate, with two senators per state. House members have two-year terms; senators have six-year staggered terms. Committees specialize in subjects, hold hearings, draft bills and conduct oversight, but they do not enact laws on their own.

sources.label: Document B · How Our Laws Are Made
sources.title: How Our Laws Are Made
sources.creator: U.S. House of Representatives
sources.excerpt: The House explains committee, chamber, reconciliation and presentation procedures; a guide describes legal procedure but not why any specific bill passes.
sources.limitation: This summary describes the linked source's scope; consult the document itself for exact language, date and purpose. Context readings are separate instructional interpretations.
sources.lessonContext: Most proposed federal laws are introduced as bills, referred for committee consideration and voted on by the House and Senate. Both chambers must generally agree to the same text before a bill is presented to the president. The president may sign or veto; a veto can be overridden by two-thirds of each chamber. Other constitutional outcomes include a bill becoming law without signature in defined circumstances and the pocket veto.

sources.label: Document C · Congressional Oversight
sources.title: Congressional Oversight
sources.creator: Congressional Research Service / Congress
sources.excerpt: Oversight can involve hearings, investigations and information demands. Congress's authority is subject to constitutional and statutory limits.
sources.limitation: This summary describes the linked source's scope; consult the document itself for exact language, date and purpose. Context readings are separate instructional interpretations.
sources.lessonContext: Congress represents constituents through lawmaking, appropriations, oversight and casework. Committees may hold hearings and request information from executive agencies. Oversight investigates whether public programs follow law and use resources appropriately; it is not automatically evidence of misconduct.

questions.prompt: A bill concerns a specialized federal transportation policy. Which procedural explanation is strongest?
choices: A committee may study and revise it, but passage still requires both chambers and applicable constitutional steps.
A committee vote alone makes it federal law.
Only senators can introduce all federal legislation.
questions.explain: The best response uses the appropriate source, legal authority, context and evidence, instead of treating a slogan or unsupported inference as proof.

questions.prompt: A news headline says the House passed a bill. What fact is still needed before stating it became law?
choices: Assume the House vote itself creates a federal statute.
Check only whether the bill has an attractive title.
Check Senate action, agreement on text and the constitutionally required presidential stage.
questions.explain: The best response uses the appropriate source, legal authority, context and evidence, instead of treating a slogan or unsupported inference as proof.

questions.prompt: A hearing witness alleges misuse of funds. What is the best next step?
choices: Assume oversight hearings themselves rewrite the funding statute.
Compare testimony with audited records and agency responses before reaching a conclusion.
Treat one allegation as a final judicial judgment.
questions.explain: The best response uses the appropriate source, legal authority, context and evidence, instead of treating a slogan or unsupported inference as proof.

questions.prompt: The House approves a bill and the Senate passes a different version. What follows before final presentation?
choices: The House version is automatically enrolled.
Both chambers must generally agree to identical final text.
A committee chairman can issue the final statute unilaterally.
questions.explain: Bicameral agreement is required.

questions.prompt: An oversight hearing includes a disputed witness claim. Which next evidence is strongest?
choices: The witness's volume and speaking speed.
The number of news clips repeating the accusation.
Agency records, documentary evidence and responses from multiple involved parties.
questions.explain: Hearings require corroboration of allegations.

questions.prompt: Which claim about congressional committees is best supported?
choices: Committees can investigate and revise bills, while enactment requires further constitutional steps.
A single committee can enact binding federal laws without either chamber.
Committees are part of the judiciary.
questions.explain: Committees support, but do not replace, congressional procedure.

sources.label: Document A · Constitution Article II
sources.title: Constitution Article II
sources.creator: Constitutional Convention
sources.excerpt: The Constitution specifies the presidency's executive role and powers including veto and commander-in-chief duties; statutory and judicial constraints also apply.
sources.limitation: This summary describes the linked source's scope; consult the document itself for exact language, date and purpose. Context readings are separate instructional interpretations.
sources.lessonContext: Article II vests federal executive power in the presidency, including executing laws, certain appointment and treaty roles, veto powers described in Article I, and commander-in-chief duties. Congress controls legislation and appropriations; courts hear legal challenges in appropriate cases. The president does not create ordinary federal statutes alone.

sources.label: Document B · Federal Register: Executive Orders
sources.title: Federal Register: Executive Orders
sources.creator: Office of the Federal Register
sources.excerpt: Executive orders are published presidential directives within asserted legal authority; they cannot override the Constitution or valid federal statutes.
sources.limitation: This summary describes the linked source's scope; consult the document itself for exact language, date and purpose. Context readings are separate instructional interpretations.
sources.lessonContext: Cabinet departments and agencies implement programs established by law, carry out enforcement and provide public services. Congress authorizes agency responsibilities and funds operations. Agencies may issue rules under delegated authority through procedures established by law; they do not possess unlimited power simply because they belong to the executive branch.

sources.label: Document C · Executive Branch
sources.title: Executive Branch
sources.creator: USAGov
sources.excerpt: Federal executive agencies implement authorized programs; their rules and decisions remain subject to other governmental checks.
sources.limitation: This summary describes the linked source's scope; consult the document itself for exact language, date and purpose. Context readings are separate instructional interpretations.
sources.lessonContext: An executive order directs federal executive operations under an asserted source of constitutional or statutory authority. Orders are recorded in the Federal Register; their legal reach depends on underlying powers and may be challenged in court. Orders cannot override the Constitution or repeal statutes passed by Congress.

questions.prompt: A president announces a permanent new federal tax in a speech. What must be evaluated?
choices: Whether the speech is longer than a congressional debate.
Whether the president's announcement means courts no longer have jurisdiction.
Whether Congress enacted legal tax authority; a presidential speech alone is not a federal tax statute.
questions.explain: The best response uses the appropriate source, legal authority, context and evidence, instead of treating a slogan or unsupported inference as proof.

questions.prompt: An agency posts a proposed regulation. Which conclusion follows?
choices: Congress has lost all oversight authority for that agency.
The proposal begins or continues a rulemaking process; it is not necessarily a binding final rule.
The agency has amended the Constitution.
questions.explain: The best response uses the appropriate source, legal authority, context and evidence, instead of treating a slogan or unsupported inference as proof.

questions.prompt: An executive order conflicts with a valid federal statute. Which assessment is strongest?
choices: An order cannot displace a valid statute; legal authority and judicial review are relevant.
Any executive order always prevails over congressional enactments.
An executive order is identical to a ratified constitutional amendment.
questions.explain: The best response uses the appropriate source, legal authority, context and evidence, instead of treating a slogan or unsupported inference as proof.

questions.prompt: A president directs an agency to act without mentioning a legal source of authority. What should a student check?
choices: The Constitution or statute authorizing the action and any applicable limits.
Whether the president has appeared on a popular quiz.
Whether the announcement contains a national flag.
questions.explain: Executive authority must rest on legal sources.

questions.prompt: Why does a Federal Register notice matter when analyzing an executive order?
choices: It automatically changes every state statute.
It provides dated official text that can be compared with the underlying law.
It proves courts cannot review the order.
questions.explain: The published text is evidence of the directive, not its unlimited legality.

questions.prompt: Congress declines to fund a proposed executive program. What does this illustrate?
choices: The president's power to appropriate funds without law.
Federal courts' sole authority over budgets.
Congressional appropriations as a constraint on executive implementation.
questions.explain: Appropriations are a legislative check.

sources.label: Document A · Constitution Article III
sources.title: Constitution Article III
sources.creator: Constitutional Convention
sources.excerpt: Article III creates the Supreme Court and authorizes a federal judiciary; Congress establishes and structures lower federal courts.
sources.limitation: This summary describes the linked source's scope; consult the document itself for exact language, date and purpose. Context readings are separate instructional interpretations.
sources.lessonContext: The Constitution creates a Supreme Court and authorizes Congress to establish lower federal courts. Federal district courts typically conduct trials and develop case records; courts of appeals review legal issues and lower-court decisions; the Supreme Court has appellate and limited original jurisdiction.

sources.label: Document B · Marbury v. Madison
sources.title: Marbury v. Madison
sources.creator: U.S. Supreme Court
sources.excerpt: Chief Justice Marshall's opinion is a foundational articulation of judicial review; the decision has a particular dispute and procedural context.
sources.limitation: This summary describes the linked source's scope; consult the document itself for exact language, date and purpose. Context readings are separate instructional interpretations.
sources.lessonContext: Judicial review is the power of courts, in cases properly before them, to evaluate whether governmental actions conflict with the Constitution. Marbury v. Madison (1803) famously articulated the Supreme Court's role in refusing to enforce unconstitutional federal law in the case before it.

sources.label: Document C · Supreme Court Landmarks
sources.title: Supreme Court Landmarks
sources.creator: Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts
sources.excerpt: Case examples illustrate how facts, questions, holdings and later interpretations differ.
sources.limitation: This summary describes the linked source's scope; consult the document itself for exact language, date and purpose. Context readings are separate instructional interpretations.
sources.lessonContext: Landmark cases are best studied through facts, constitutional question, holding and consequences. Brown v. Board of Education (1954) rejected state-mandated racial segregation in public schools, while Tinker v. Des Moines (1969) addressed student political expression at school. These cases concern different rights and different contexts.

questions.prompt: A witness disputes facts in a federal case. Which court ordinarily hears testimony and develops a trial record?
choices: A congressional committee acting as the final criminal court.
A federal district court with jurisdiction.
The Supreme Court in every case.
questions.explain: The best response uses the appropriate source, legal authority, context and evidence, instead of treating a slogan or unsupported inference as proof.

questions.prompt: A court rules a statute unconstitutional in a properly presented case. What principle does this illustrate?
choices: Judicial review, subject to jurisdiction and constitutional reasoning.
The court's authority to amend Article V on its own.
The president's power to nullify any judicial decision.
questions.explain: The best response uses the appropriate source, legal authority, context and evidence, instead of treating a slogan or unsupported inference as proof.

questions.prompt: A student claims Tinker means schools may never regulate student expression. What should the student do?
choices: Rely on the word freedom without reading the opinion.
Apply Brown's school-segregation holding as the direct rule on every speech issue.
